q-106:
We add the corresponding entries:

$$
\begin{aligned}M+N & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & 14 \\ 2 & 9 & -13\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-15 & -6 & -13 \\ -1 & -8 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3+(-15) & -6+(-6) & 14+(-13) \\ 2+(-1) & 9+(-8) & -13+14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & -12 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-72382:
We note that $5{x}^{4}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the radical. So we make a substitution

$$
u=1+{x}^{5}.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =5{x}^{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{1/2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{1/2}}{(\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =2{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =2\sqrt{u}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=1+{x}^{5}$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-2195:
We note that $2x$ is the derivative of the quantity in the parentheses. So we make a substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}+1.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x({x}^{2}+1)^{12}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}+1)^{12}\,2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{12}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\int {u}^{12}\,\text{d}u=\frac{{u}^{13}}{13}+C
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u={x}^{2}+1$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 2x({x}^{2}+1)^{12}\,\text{d}x=\frac{({x}^{2}+1)^{13}}{13}+C.
$$

q-72467:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-5).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-5.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-5}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{{x}^{2}-5}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{({x}^{2}-5)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-12496:
In this case, the ${x}^{3}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{4}+11).$ But the derivative is $4{x}^{3},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{4}+11.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u={x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}{({x}^{4}+11)}^{9}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{4}+11)^{9}\cdot {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{9}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{9}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{9}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{10}}{10}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{40}{u}^{10}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{40}({x}^{4}+11)^{10}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-49451:
Let $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-72605:
Let $u=2-5{x}^{5}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-25{x}^{4}\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{25})\text{d}u={x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{10{x}^{4}}{2-5{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x & =10\int \frac{1}{2-5{x}^{5}}\cdot {x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{25})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{10}{25}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2-5{x}^{5}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-113726:
Let $u=3-{x}^{5}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5{x}^{4}\,⟹\,-\frac{7}{5}\text{d}u=7{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7{x}^{4}}{{(3-{x}^{5})}^{6}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{(3-{x}^{5})}^{6}}\cdot 7{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{6}}\cdot (-\frac{7}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{6}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{7}{5}(-\frac{1}{5{u}^{5}})+C \\  & =\frac{7}{25{u}^{5}}+C \\  & =\frac{7}{25(3-{x}^{5})^{5}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-12502:
Let $u={x}^{2}+5.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{({x}^{2}+5)}^{10}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{({x}^{2}+5)}^{10}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{10}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{10}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{9{u}^{9}})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18{u}^{9}}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18({x}^{2}+5)^{9}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-46831:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{{x}^{2}-4} & =\frac{\sqrt{2+2}-2}{{2}^{2}-4}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{x+2}-2}{(x-2)(x+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{x+2}-2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{{(\sqrt{x+2})}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x+2-4}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x-2}{(x-2)(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{1}{(x+2)(\sqrt{x+2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(2+2)(\sqrt{2+2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-46830:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=4$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{x-4}{\sqrt{3x-3}-3} & =\frac{4-4}{\sqrt{3(4)-3}-3}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{x-4}{\sqrt{3x-3}-3} & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{(x-4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{(\sqrt{3x-3}-3)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{(x-4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{{(\sqrt{3x-3})}^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{(x-4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{3x-3-9} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{(x-4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{3x-12} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{(x-4)(\sqrt{3x-3}+3)}{3(x-4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{3x-3}+3}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3(4)-3}+3}{3} \\  & =\frac{3+3}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-66896:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-1} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-10484:
To find the $y$-intercepts of the hyperbola, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}25{y}^{2}-9{x}^{2} & =225 \\ 25{y}^{2}-9(0)^{2} & =225 \\ 25{y}^{2} & =225 \\ {y}^{2} & =9 \\ y & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $y$-intercepts are $(0,\pm 3).$

q-84045:
To find the $y$-intercepts of the hyperbola, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the hyperbola and solve for $y,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{9}-\frac{(y-5)^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ \frac{(0+3)^{2}}{9}-\frac{(y-5)^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ 1-\frac{(y-5)^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ -\frac{(y-5)^{2}}{25} & =0 \\ (y-5)^{2} & =0 \\ y-5 & =0 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $y$-intercept is $(0,5).$

q-8220:
To find the complex conjugate, we flip the sign of the imaginary part.

In the given number $z=3+5\text{i},$ the imaginary part is $5\text{i}.$ Flipping the sign, we get $-5\text{i}.$

Therefore, the complex conjugate is given by $\overset{―}{z}=3-5\text{i}.$

q-16414:
To find the complex conjugate, we flip the sign of the imaginary part.

In the given number $z=5-12\text{i},$ the imaginary part is $-12\text{i}.$ Flipping the sign, we get $12\text{i}.$

Therefore, the complex conjugate is given by $\overset{―}{z}=5+12\text{i}.$
